newsitem.title: USA: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Fed leaves interest rates unchanged.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday amid signs that the economy is on course for modest growth with stable inflation next year.
The decision by the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee had been widely expected and had only a fleeting impact on financial markets.
"The Federal Open Market Committee meeting ended at 12:25 p.m. 1725 GMT. There is no further announcement," central bank spokesman Joseph Coyne said in a brief statement.

After growing at a brisk 4.7 percent annual rate in the second quarter, the economy slowed to a 2.2 percent growth rate in the third quarter, a pace that most analysts reckon is sustainable on a long-term basis without fanning inflation.
"The Fed wanted to get growth down and their wish came true," said Chris Rupkey, vice president at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi in New York.
Curbing inflation is considered critical to prolonging the economic expansion that began in March 1991 and now is in its sixth year without showing signs of serious flagging.

A survey of about 50 top private economists released this week found that on average they expect the economy to grow by 2.2 percent in 1997 after expanding 2.4 percent this year. Consumer prices were seen rising by 3 percent in 1997, after increasing by 2.9 percent this year.
The Labour Department said Wednesday that producer prices rose at their fastest clip in seven months in October, jumping 0.4 percent after a 0.2 percent increase in September.
But the rise was totally due to surging prices for food and energy. After stripping out those volatile costs, producer prices actually fell last month, by 0.3 percent.
"There's not a lot of inflation," said Sally Kleinman, senior economist at Wall Street broker Chase Securities.

That is good news for the financial markets. Stock prices edged up to another record close on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares rising 8.20 points to 6,274.24. Bond prices were marginally lower.
Only a month or so ago many Wall Street firms were arguing that the Fed needed to raise short-term interest rates to cool off an economy that seemed to be on the verge of over-heating.

But the slowdown since then has taken the pressure off the central bank to act to restrain growth. Most analysts expect it to decide again to hold rates steady at its next policy-making meeting on Dec. 17.
But that does not mean that the central bank is about to let down its guard against inflation.
At 5.2 percent, the unemployment rate is hovering near a 7-1/2-year low and is at a level that in the past has presaged stepped-up wage demands from workers, and higher inflation.
That is why some analysts believe the Fed secretly decided Wednesday to continue to lean in the direction of increasing rates if necessary to contain inflation.
Many -- but by no means, all -- analysts believe the Fed will indeed need to raise rates next year to keep inflation in check and the economy on course for continued expansion.
"The next move will likely be a tightening," said John Williams, managing director at Bankers Trust in New York. "The economy is going to reaccelerate toward the end of this year and into next."

The central bank has not changed rates since January, when it trimmed both the federal funds and discount rates by a quarter percentage point to help the economy through what Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan called "a soft patch."
The federal funds rate, which commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans, currently stands at 5.25 percent. The discount rate, which the Fed charges banks for cash, is at 5 percent.
